John Preston
PRES-tun
proper noun
From the surname Preston; the Puritan divine, master of Emmanuel College and preacher of the covenant of grace.

📖 Biblical Definition

John Preston was a Puritan divine of the early seventeenth century, master of Emmanuel College in Cambridge and one of the most powerful preachers of his day, who carried the gospel even into the court of King James and King Charles. His chief theme was the covenant of grace and the life of faith, set forth in his books The New Covenant and The Breastplate of Faith and Love. He preached the everlasting covenant that God establishes with His people and their seed, to be a God unto them (Gen 17:7), the new covenant in which the Lord writes His laws upon the heart and is their God and they His people (Heb 8:10). He pressed home that the blessing of Abraham comes upon the Gentiles through Christ, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith (Gal 3:14), and that to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness (Rom 4:5). The dictionary honours Preston as a master of covenant theology and a preacher who drew sinners to rest upon the free grace of God in Christ. He taught the troubled soul to look not to its own worthiness but to the covenant and the promise, and to take hold of God by faith as a God in covenant who cannot deny Himself.

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 8:10 — "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people:"

Gen 17:7 — "And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee."

Rom 4:5 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Gal 3:14 — "That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

He preached the covenant of grace and the life of faith, drawing sinners to rest on God’s free promise, not their own worth.

expand to see more

The error Preston preached against was the bondage of a religion of works and the despair of a soul looking to its own worthiness. He set before sinners the covenant of grace, the everlasting covenant in which God binds Himself to be a God to His people and to write His law upon their hearts. The dictionary honours this covenant theology, which casts the trembling soul wholly upon the free promise of God in Christ.

What is honourable in Preston is that he made the covenant the ground of faith and assurance. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the believer rests not on his own worthiness but on the God who justifieth the ungodly, whose faith is counted for righteousness. Preston taught the troubled to take hold of God by faith as a God in covenant who cannot deny Himself, and so to find peace not in themselves but in the promise. This is the very marrow of the gospel the Reformation recovered.
